one_liner: Portable, no_std Rust 64-bit non-crypto hash; ~11x FNV-1a and ~16% over MurmurHash3 bulk, but slower than xxHash64/XXH3.
what_it_does: SeaHash is a 64-bit non-cryptographic hash whose output is independent of endianness and pointer width, so the author pitches it for on-disk checksums as well as hash tables. The API is two one-shot functions, seahash::hash(&[u8]) -> u64 and hash_seeded(buf, a, b, c, d) with four u64 seeds, plus a streaming SeaHasher that implements core::hash::Hasher (and io::Write with the use_std feature). It is not a drop-in for C/C++ code: the canonical implementation is a Rust crate, and SMHasher tests a separate C port.
how_it_is_fast: It reads 8 bytes per load and keeps four independent 64-bit lanes, consuming 32 bytes per loop iteration, so the four multiply chains can overlap through instruction-level parallelism; the lanes are only XOR-combined at the end with the length. Each lane update is XOR-then-diffuse, where the diffusion is a PCG-style permutation: multiply by 0x6eed0e9da4d94a4f, xor-shift by a data-dependent amount ((x >> 32) >> (x >> 60)), multiply again. The construction is a 4-lane, length-padded Merkle-Damgard scheme with no SIMD or hardware intrinsics, so its speed comes from scalar multiply throughput alone.
when_to_use: You are replacing FNV-1a/FNV-64 or byte-at-a-time hashing of multi-KB buffers in Rust: SMHasher's bulk test puts it at about 8.2 GB/s versus about 0.75 GB/s for FNV.

You need a hash value that is the same on little- and big-endian and on 32- and 64-bit targets (for example content checksums or dedup keys persisted to disk), and you can pin the crate's major version.
no_std or embedded Rust where you want zero runtime dependencies, no unsafe SIMD paths, and a small auditable codebase.
You already have data or file formats keyed by SeaHash values and need a maintained-enough Rust implementation to keep reading them.
when_not_to_use: Raw speed is the goal: in the same SMHasher table xxHash64 (11,177 MiB/s), MetroHash64, City64 and XXH3 (20,854 MiB/s) are all faster in bulk, which contradicts the README's '3-20% faster than xxHash/MetroHash' claim.

Small keys: SMHasher averages 58.6 cycles/hash for 1-31 byte keys, worse than MurmurHash3F (52.7) and xxHash64 (49.7); keys whose length is not a multiple of 8 cost about 61 cycles versus 36-41 for 8/16/24/32-byte keys.

Anything exposed to attacker-chosen keys: the doc comment says the seed can be extracted with some computational work and tells you to use it only with a fallback such as SipHash; SMHasher also flags a PerlinNoise failure (seed/key collisions).

ARM targets without measuring first: open issue #7 reports it about 10% slower than SipHash on a Cortex-A55 (versus about 1.5x faster on an Intel Skylake), and the docs say non-ideal architectures lose up to 30-40%.
Projects that need an actively maintained crate: the last code change was December 2020 (v4.1.0, January 2021), and later commits only added the license text.

integration.dependencies: none (quickcheck and criterion are dev-dependencies only)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (no rust-version or edition key in Cargo.toml, so edition 2015; the code uses const fn with let bindings, which needs a Rust from roughly 2019 onward)
integration.platforms: any Rust target, no_std by default; tuned for 64-bit little-endian (32-bit targets split each 8-byte read into two u32 reads)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; hash()/hash_seeded() are pure functions and SeaHasher is a plain Copy struct with no shared state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — as a Rust Hasher it can replace an FNV hasher via BuildHasherDefault<SeaHasher>, but the crate ships no BuildHasher type (open issue #14), and C/C++ users need an unofficial port

gotchas: Output is only promised to be stable within a major version: the docs say values change only on major bumps, and 4.0 changed the streaming hasher to fix chunking sensitivity (issues #1, #5). Pin the major version for anything persisted.

hash_seeded takes four u64 seeds that directly initialise the lanes. For inputs under 8 bytes, the input is XORed into lane a with the seed, so a key and a seed are interchangeable through XOR. Seeding is obfuscation, not DoS protection.

The streaming SeaHasher implements write_u8/u32/u64 and similar by routing the bytes through the generic byte-buffer path. Hashing integer keys in a HashMap therefore pays tail-buffer bookkeeping on every call.

The hot loops use unsafe raw-pointer reads (read_unaligned since the fix for issue #9). The benchmark tables in the docs (0.24 cycles/byte, CityHash 1.62 cpb, '2.5 GHz CPU') date from 2016 and give no compiler, flags or competitor code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over xxHash, wyhash or the rapidhash Rust port only when you specifically need SeaHash-compatible or endian/width-independent persisted values from a dependency-free no_std Rust crate. Those siblings post roughly 1.4-2.7x its bulk throughput in the same SMHasher table, and for in-memory Rust HashMaps foldhash, rustc-hash or aHash are the catalogued choices.
verified_claims_summary: The only independent numbers are from rurban/SMHasher, which tests a C port (seahash.c, seed XORed into lane a) on its default AMD Ryzen 5 3350G table with no compiler or flags stated. Bulk speed on 256 KiB keys was 8,240.58 MiB/s versus 754.70 for FNV1a (~11x) and 7,104.08 for Murmur3F (~1.16x), but it lost to xxHash64 (11,176.72) and xxh3 (20,853.74). On small keys it averaged 58.61 cycles/hash, beating FNV1a (75.28) but not Murmur3F (52.69); the Rust crate's own criterion bench times SeaHash alone.
status_note: Stale: code last changed in December 2020 and v4.1.0 (January 2021) is the latest crate, yet it still has about 153M crates.io downloads; the crate is MIT, dependency-free and a few hundred lines, so it is easy to vendor.
